summary: Defines a protocol for carrying ISDN Q.921 user messages over IP using SCTP, between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 4233.

plainLanguage.summary: Old phone-network messages can be wrapped up and sent across the Internet between two machines. This says how to wrap them. A newer document later replaced it.

subtitle: How an ISDN signaling gateway hands Q.921 user messages to a controller across an IP network using SCTP.

tldr.problem: ISDN signaling arrives at a Signaling Gateway over a standard ISDN interface, but the call processing happens on a separate Media Gateway Controller reached over IP.
tldr.mechanism: The gateway terminates Q.921 and backhauls the Q.921 user layer (such as Q.931) to the controller inside IUA messages carried over SCTP. IUA also tracks which controller processes are up and active, and supports fail-over and load sharing.
tldr.outcome: IUA gives a standard way to split ISDN signaling across IP. This RFC is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 4233.

today: RFC 3057 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4233 and was updated by RFC 3807. Use RFC 4233 for the current IUA specification.

sections.title: Backhauling ISDN Signaling
sections.content:
In this RFC, Q.921-User means any upper layer that uses Q.921 services, for example Q.931 or QSIG. A Signaling Gateway (SG) receives ISDN signaling over a standard ISDN interface and terminates Q.921. It then backhauls the Q.921 user layer to a Media Gateway Controller (MGC) for call processing.

The delivery mechanism has three jobs: carry the Q.921/Q.931 boundary primitives, support communication between Layer Management modules on the two sides, and manage the active associations between SG and MGC. Both Primary Rate and Basic Rate access are covered, in point-to-point and point-to-multipoint modes. QSIG needs no different handling, so the text only mentions Q.931.

IUA is recommended to run over SCTP. The RFC lists packet-oriented delivery, sequenced delivery within multiple streams, multi-homing, resistance to flooding and masquerade attacks, and path-MTU-aware segmentation as the reasons. Where there is no redundancy requirement, TCP can be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone switch hears the signals on the line but passes them to a different computer that decides what to do with each call. IUA is the envelope used to send those signals between the two.

sections.title: Gateways, Servers and Fail-over
sections.content:
An Application Server (AS) is a logical entity, modeled at the SG as an ordered list of Application Server Processes (ASPs), such as primary and backup controller instances. Each incoming Q.921-User message is assigned to a unique AS based on its Interface Identifier, which names the physical interface at the SG. Its values are of local significance only.

The model supports n+k redundancy: n ASPs are the minimum needed to carry traffic, and k are available to take over. 1+1 active/standby and 1+0 with no redundancy are subsets. The RFC recommends at least two ASPs on separate hosts and no single point of failure in the network. Sharing call state between ASPs is outside the scope.

By default the SG acts as server and the ASP as client, so ASPs initiate the SCTP association. The registered port for IUA is 9900. It is recommended to use a separate SCTP stream for each D channel.
sections.plainLanguage: If the main helper falls ill, a backup helper takes over so calls keep going. The gateway keeps a list of helpers and knows which one is working right now.

sections.title: IUA Messages and Headers
sections.content:
Every message starts with a common header: Version (value 1 means Release 1.0), a Reserved byte, Message Class, Message Type and Message Length, all in network byte order. After that come parameters in Tag-Length-Value form. Each parameter must be padded to a multiple of 4 bytes, and the padding is not counted in the length.

The classes IUA uses are Management (0), ASP State Maintenance (3), ASP Traffic Maintenance (4) and Q.921/Q.931 Boundary Primitives Transport (5). The transport messages (Data, Unit Data, Establish, Release) carry an IUA header with the Interface Identifier (integer tag 0x1 or text tag 0x3) and a DLCI made of a SAPI and a TEI, coded as in Q.921. Integer identifiers must be supported; text ones are optional.

Data requests carry acknowledged information transfer and Unit Data the unacknowledged kind. The MGC controls the state of the D channel by sending an Establish Request when it wants the channel in service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a short label saying what kind it is, how long it is and which phone line it is about. The rest is the signal being passed along.

sections.title: ASP and AS States
sections.content:
The SG tracks every ASP in one of three states. ASP-DOWN is where all ASPs start and no IUA messages should be sent. ASP-INACTIVE means the peer is up but traffic is stopped. ASP-ACTIVE means traffic flows.

The ASP moves forward with its own messages. After the SCTP association is up it sends ASP Up and must wait for ASP Up Ack. It then sends ASP Active, with a Traffic Mode Type of Over-ride (the ASP takes all traffic, as in primary/backup) or Load-share (the ASP shares traffic with other active ASPs), and waits for ASP Active Ack before sending data. An ASP may resend ASP Up every 2 seconds if unanswered.

The AS has four states: AS-DOWN, AS-INACTIVE, AS-ACTIVE and AS-PENDING. When the last active ASP leaves, the AS goes to AS-PENDING, a recovery timer T(r) starts and the SG queues incoming messages. If an ASP becomes active before T(r) expires the queue goes to it; otherwise the queued messages are discarded.

Optional Heartbeat messages can be used where the transport has no heartbeat of its own. If nothing arrives within 2*T(beat), the peer is considered down.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper first says it is awake, then says it is ready for work. If the only working helper quits, the gateway holds the messages for a short while in case another helper steps up.

sections.title: Errors, Notifications and TEI Status
sections.content:
Management messages travel on SCTP stream 0, which should be used so ordering is kept. The Error message carries an Error Code such as Invalid Version (0x01), Invalid Interface Identifier (0x02), Unsupported Traffic Handling Mode (0x05), Unexpected Message (0x06), Unassigned TEI (0x0a) and Unrecognized SAPI (0x0b). Optional diagnostic information could include the first 40 bytes of the offending message.

The Notify message reports an AS state change (AS_Down, AS_Inactive, AS_Active, AS_Pending) or Other events: insufficient ASP resources in load-share mode, or that an alternate ASP became active. Notify does not force an ASP to act; ASPs stay in control of what they do.

TEI Status messages let the Layer Management on each side learn whether a TEI is assigned or unassigned by Q.921, because Layer 2 and Layer 3 management are no longer co-located when ISDN is backhauled.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, a short note says what, such as wrong phone line or unknown caller number. Another note tells helpers who is on duty.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
IUA carries telephony signaling, so it must involve the security needs of end users, network providers and applications. Its objectives are availability, integrity and confidentiality of user data transport. IUA runs over SCTP, which provides protection against blind denial of service attacks, flooding, masquerade and improper monopolization of services.

In a managed single-operator network, an appropriate security policy is expected. Where several parties are involved, the RFC recommends IPsec to protect the confidentiality of user payload. For cases such as masking IP addresses and ports, IPsec ESP should be used, with ISAKMP for key management.

For IANA, the RFC asks for an SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier of 1 for IUA and sets IETF Consensus as the rule for new message classes, types and parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone signals are private, so the pipe they travel through must be hard to attack. When many companies share a network, an extra lock called IPsec is recommended.
